title: Impression: Paris, 1874
subtitle: The Société anonyme exhibition at 35 boulevard des Capucines, its critics, its debts and its sequel, Paris, 1873–1876
intro: On 27 December 1873 a group of painters who were tired of waiting on the Salon jury signed a charter for a joint-stock company: the Société anonyme coopérative des artistes peintres, sculpteurs, graveurs, etc. Monet, Renoir, Sisley, Degas, Morisot and Pissarro were among the first signers. They had no jury and no prizes. Each member paid a subscription, the hanging was settled by lot within groups of similar size, and the society took a commission on sales. Four months later, on 15 April 1874, they opened a month-long show in the empty rooms of the photographer Nadar's former studio at 35 boulevard des Capucines. It ran two weeks ahead of the official Salon, which opened on 1 May at the Palais de l'Industrie.

About thirty artists showed some 165 catalogued works. Visitors paid one franc and could come in the evening as well as by day. The best-known pictures now are Monet's harbour at Le Havre, catalogued as 'Impression, soleil levant', Morisot's 'Le Berceau', Renoir's 'La Loge', Cézanne's 'La Maison du pendu' and 'Une moderne Olympia', and Degas's dancers and racecourses. Roughly 3,500 people came, against several hundred thousand at the Salon, and only a handful of works sold. On 25 April Louis Leroy's satire in Le Charivari turned Monet's title into a joke name, 'impressionists'. Four days later Jules Castagnary used the same word seriously in Le Siècle. In December the members voted to wind the company up.

This chapter lays those days out through the people who left a dated record of them, and most of that record is letters, published reviews and accounts, not diaries. The painters wrote letters to friends, dealers and family: Pissarro to Théodore Duret, Cézanne to his mother, Morisot to her sister and her mother. Degas wrote to Tissot, and Renoir and Rouart wrote to Caillebotte. The critics wrote in public, on fixed dates. Edmond de Goncourt kept the one true diary here, and he visited Degas's studio two months before the opening. The society's own accounts, its rent, lamp oil, upholstery, police and catalogue sales, survive as a financial statement dated 27 May 1874. Paul Durand-Ruel's memoirs and the painters' late interviews were written decades afterwards. They are flagged as such, because several of the best-known anecdotes, including Monet's story of how 'Impression' got its title, come from them.

Seen together, the eyes show how small the event was at the time and how quickly it became a myth. Morisot was the only woman in the show. Her old teacher wrote to her mother that her work had been hung in poisonous company. Her future brother-in-law Manet refused to join and took his chances with the Salon jury. Pissarro had buried his young daughter days before the opening and called the show a success. Cézanne sold a picture to a count and told his mother that he still had to keep working. The chapter follows the year to the Hôtel Drouot auction of 24 March 1875, where the police were called to keep order. It closes with the second group exhibition at Durand-Ruel's gallery in spring 1876, where the critic Albert Wolff mocked them again and Philippe Burty reported on them to English readers.

One question stays open. Monet signed and dated his harbour picture '72'. Astronomical and tidal work published by the Musée Marmottan in 2014 points to the morning of 13 November 1872. Some earlier catalogues dated it to 1873 and assumed the '72' was an error or added later. The book reports both positions.
calendar_note: All dates are in the Gregorian calendar. Newspaper reviews carry their issue dates, and French dailies often appeared dated the following day, so a review given here as 24 April may be cited elsewhere as 25 April. Several letters, including Degas's to Tissot and Guichard's to Madame Morisot, are undated in the original. Editors have placed them by their contents, and they are marked approx.

eyes.name: Berthe Morisot
eyes.role: Painter, aged 33 in 1874; signatory of the Société charter and the only woman in the first exhibition; from December 1874 the wife of Eugène Manet
eyes.side: Société anonyme exhibitors; the Morisot and Manet families
eyes.where: Rue Franklin, Passy, Paris; summers on the Normandy coast; Isle of Wight in 1875
eyes.vantage_label: exhibitor and the only woman on the walls
eyes.form: dated letters (her own and her family's)
eyes.authenticity: Her letters and those of her mother, her sister Edma and her teacher Joseph Guichard were edited by Denis Rouart, Correspondance de Berthe Morisot (Paris, 1950; English translation 1957). Many are undated, and the editors placed them by their contents. The originals remain largely in family hands.
eyes.bio: Morisot trained under Guichard and Corot and had shown at the Salon since 1864. In 1874 she chose to join the independent show against the advice of Manet, Guichard and her family. Her letters record the warnings of the people around her and the cost of her choice.

sources.title: Musée d'Orsay: Le Berceau (1872)
Ministère de la Culture: 1874 – Première exposition

eyes.name: Claude Monet
eyes.role: Landscape painter, aged 33; living at Argenteuil; one of the moving spirits of the Société
eyes.where: Argenteuil, with visits to Le Havre and Paris
eyes.vantage_label: exhibitor whose title named the movement
eyes.authenticity: His letters are catalogued in Daniel Wildenstein's catalogue raisonné. Few survive from spring 1874 itself. The story of how the title 'Impression' was chosen comes from Monet's interview with Maurice Guillemot in La Revue illustrée, 1898, a quarter-century later. It is reported as his recollection.
eyes.bio: Monet had proposed a group show as early as the late 1860s. In 1874 he hung a harbour sunrise whose catalogue title gave the critics their word. His letters of these years are mostly appeals for money, and they show how little the exhibition changed his finances.

sources.title: Musée Marmottan Monet: Impression, soleil levant
Texas State University press release on dating the painting (2014)

eyes.name: Camille Pissarro
eyes.role: Landscape painter, aged 43; the oldest of the core group; living at Pontoise with Julie Vellay and their children
eyes.vantage_label: founder who argued for the co-operative form
eyes.authenticity: His letters are edited by Janine Bailly-Herzberg, Correspondance de Camille Pissarro, vol. 1 (1980). The letter to Théodore Duret of 5 May 1874 is dated in the original.
eyes.bio: Pissarro modelled the society on a bakers' union charter he knew from Pontoise. He insisted that his friends Cézanne and Guillaumin be included. Of all the founders he believed most strongly in the group as a collective.

sources.title: Kunstmuseum Basel: Pissarro biography (PDF)
Clark Art Institute: Pissarro's People – Minette

eyes.name: Edgar Degas
eyes.role: Painter of dancers, racecourses and laundresses, aged 39; chief recruiter of exhibitors
eyes.authenticity: The letters are edited in Marcel Guérin, Lettres de Degas (1931; English 1947). The letter urging James Tissot to exhibit is undated, and editors place it in early 1874 from its contents.
eyes.bio: Degas wanted the show to include respectable Salon painters, so that it could not be dismissed as a salon of rejects. He signed up de Nittis, Lepic and others and tried hard to win over Tissot and Manet. His studio was the subject of Goncourt's best-known entry of 1874.

sources.title: Impressionists Gallery: Degas chronology
Degas catalogue raisonné (Schulman): bibliography

eyes.name: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
eyes.role: Figure painter, aged 33; member of the hanging committee; later chair of the liquidation meeting
eyes.where: Studio at 35 rue Saint-Georges, Paris; Argenteuil in summer
eyes.vantage_label: hanger, host of the liquidation, instigator of the auction
eyes.form: dated letters; later recollections recorded by others
eyes.authenticity: Few letters by Renoir survive from 1874–76. The letter of 5 February 1876 to Caillebotte, co-signed with Rouart, is dated. Most anecdotes about the hanging and the auction come from Ambroise Vollard's book on Renoir (1919/1920) and Jean Renoir's memoir of his father (1962). Both were written much later and are treated as recollection.
eyes.bio: Renoir helped hang the 1874 show, and his brother Edmond edited the catalogue. In December he hosted the meeting that dissolved the society. In March 1875 he pushed for the auction at the Hôtel Drouot, where his own canvases fetched some of the lowest prices.

sources.title: Courtauld Gallery: La Loge (1874)
Ministère de la Culture: 1876 – Deuxième exposition

eyes.name: Paul Cézanne
eyes.role: Painter, aged 35; working beside Pissarro at Auvers-sur-Oise; admitted to the show at Pissarro's insistence
eyes.where: Auvers-sur-Oise and Paris; Aix-en-Provence later in 1874
eyes.vantage_label: the exhibitor critics laughed at most
eyes.authenticity: His letters are edited by John Rewald, Paul Cézanne: Correspondance (1937; revised editions). The letter to his mother of 26 September 1874 is dated.
eyes.bio: Some founders were wary of Cézanne, and Pissarro and Monet argued for him. His 'Une moderne Olympia' was a hot-tempered answer to Manet's Olympia, and it drew the harshest jokes in the press. Even so, 'La Maison du pendu' was one of the few works sold.

sources.title: Musée d'Orsay: La Maison du pendu, Auvers-sur-Oise
Musée d'Orsay: Une moderne Olympia

eyes.name: Édouard Manet
eyes.role: Painter, aged 42; the older figure the group looked to, who refused to exhibit with them
eyes.side: The official Salon (by choice); friend of the group
eyes.where: Studio at 4 rue de Saint-Pétersbourg, Paris; Gennevilliers and Argenteuil in summer 1874
eyes.vantage_label: the friend who stayed with the Salon
eyes.authenticity: Manet's letters are scattered across several editions (Juliet Wilson-Bareau, Manet by Himself, 1991, gathers many). The Salon catalogue of 1874 records his accepted entry, and his 1876 studio show is documented by its printed invitation and press notices.
eyes.bio: Manet thought the Salon was the only battlefield that counted. He declined Degas's invitation and lent no work of his own, although he had lent a Morisot. In 1874 the jury accepted one of his three entries and rejected two. That summer he painted beside Monet and Renoir at Argenteuil, and in December his brother Eugène married Berthe Morisot.

sources.title: NGA wall texts, Paris 1874: The Impressionist Moment (PDF)

eyes.name: Edmond de Goncourt
eyes.role: Novelist, collector and diarist, aged 51; keeping the Journal alone since his brother Jules's death in 1870
eyes.side: Paris literary world; collector of Japanese art
eyes.where: His house at Auteuil; visiting studios in Paris
eyes.vantage_label: diarist in the studio before the show
eyes.authenticity: The Journal des Goncourt was published by Edmond himself in nine volumes (1887–96) in a trimmed and revised form. The complete text appeared only from 1956. Entries quoted here are from the volume covering 1872–77 (second series, vol. 2).
eyes.bio: Goncourt's novel Manette Salomon (1867) had already called for painters of modern life. He came to Degas's studio as a judge and left believing that Degas had found the subject he had himself been arguing for. He did not report on the exhibition itself.

sources.title: Journal des Goncourt, 2e série, vol. 2 (1872–1877), Project Gutenberg #17420 (via Online Books Page)

eyes.name: Émile Zola
eyes.role: Novelist and art critic, aged 34; Cézanne's boyhood friend and Manet's defender since 1866
eyes.side: Republican press; friend of the group
eyes.where: Batignolles, Paris; writing for Le Sémaphore de Marseille and the St Petersburg monthly Vestnik Evropy
eyes.vantage_label: friendly critic writing for distant readers
eyes.language: French (the Vestnik Evropy pieces appeared in Russian translation)
eyes.authenticity: His Sémaphore de Marseille columns and the Paris letters he wrote for Vestnik Evropy (Le Messager de l'Europe) are collected in modern editions of his Écrits sur l'art. Most were unsigned or appeared in translation at the time.
eyes.bio: Zola knew nearly everyone in the group from the Café Guerbois years. His reports on them went to readers far from Paris, in Marseille and in Russia. He covered the 1875 auction for Marseille and the 1876 show for St Petersburg.

sources.title: Ministère de la Culture: 1876 – Deuxième exposition (cites Zola, Sémaphore de Marseille, 27 March 1875)

eyes.name: Louis Leroy
eyes.role: Engraver, painter and playwright, aged 61; satirical art critic of Le Charivari
eyes.where: Paris; the rooms at 35 boulevard des Capucines
eyes.authenticity: The review 'L'Exposition des impressionnistes', Le Charivari, 25 April 1874, survives in the paper's run (digitised on Gallica). Its dialogue form and the academic painter 'Joseph Vincent' are Leroy's invention, and it is read as satire, not reportage.
eyes.bio: Leroy had trained as an engraver and shown at the Salon himself. He wrote the piece as a comic walk through the rooms with an imaginary old landscape painter who is driven mad by what he sees. The joke gave the group the name it is still known by.

sources.title: Ministère de la Culture: 1874 – Première exposition

eyes.name: Jules-Antoine Castagnary
eyes.role: Republican critic and journalist, aged 43; champion of Courbet and of naturalism; later Director of Fine Arts (1887)
eyes.where: Paris; the rooms at 35 boulevard des Capucines
eyes.authenticity: 'Exposition du boulevard des Capucines: les impressionnistes', Le Siècle, 29 April 1874, survives in the newspaper's run.
eyes.bio: Castagnary had spent years defending painters of the real against the academy. Four days after Leroy he took the joke word and gave it a serious definition. He also predicted that the group would not last as a group.

sources.title: Hérodote: Paris 1874, inventer l'impressionnisme

eyes.name: Philippe Burty
eyes.role: Critic, print connoisseur and collector of Japanese art, aged 43; writer for La République française
eyes.side: Republican press; friend of the group
eyes.where: Paris; the rooms at 35 boulevard des Capucines and the Hôtel Drouot
eyes.form: dated reviews and a catalogue preface
eyes.authenticity: His reviews in La République française (1874), his preface to the Drouot sale catalogue (March 1875) and his London report 'The Exhibition of the Intransigeants' (The Academy, 15 April 1876) are dated publications. Secondary accounts give the date of the first 1874 review differently, as 16, 24 or 25 April.
eyes.bio: Burty knew the printmakers among the exhibitors well and wrote in the Gambettist republican paper. He was close to the Goncourts. He is usually credited with coining 'japonisme' in 1872. He supported the painters three times in public: the 1874 show, the 1875 sale and the 1876 show.

sources.title: Degas catalogue raisonné: Burty, 'The Exhibition of the Intransigeants', 15 April 1876

eyes.name: Paul Durand-Ruel
eyes.role: Picture dealer, aged 42; had bought heavily from Monet and Pissarro since meeting them in London in 1871
eyes.where: His gallery, rue Laffitte / 11 rue Le Peletier, Paris
eyes.authenticity: His memoirs were written in old age and first published by Lionello Venturi in Les Archives de l'impressionnisme (1939). They are vivid and self-justifying, and they were written long after the events, so they are flagged as recollection.
eyes.bio: The 1873 slump forced Durand-Ruel to stop buying, and the painters' need for a public of their own grew partly out of that. He took no part in the 1874 show. He helped with the 1875 auction and lent his own gallery for the second exhibition in 1876.

sources.title: Ministère de la Culture: 1876 – Deuxième exposition (cites his recollection of the 1875 sale)

eyes.name: Société anonyme coopérative des artistes peintres, sculpteurs, graveurs, etc. (charter, catalogue and accounts)
eyes.role: The artists' joint-stock company: its charter, printed catalogue, financial statement and minutes
eyes.where: 35 boulevard des Capucines (exhibition); meetings in members' studios
eyes.authenticity: The charter of 27 December 1873, the printed catalogue (nos 1–165, with gaps), and the financial statement of 27 May 1874 survive and are reproduced in modern studies, notably Charles S. Moffett (ed.), The New Painting: Impressionism 1874–1886 (1986). The figures given here follow the Ministry of Culture's summary of those documents.
eyes.bio: The paperwork shows plainly what the painters thought they were making: a company with shares, a commission on sales and rules for hanging by lot. Its accounts record what the venture cost and how few people paid to see it.

sources.title: Ministère de la Culture: 1874 – Première exposition
National Gallery of Art: 1874, the birth of Impressionism

entries.place: Le Havre, a hotel window above the outer harbour
entries.headline: A grey-blue harbour, an orange sun, a few strokes
entries.digest: Monet painted the harbour of his home town from a high window. The cranes and masts are thin blue-grey marks in the mist, a small rowing boat sits dark in the foreground, and an orange disc throws a broken streak of reflection across the water. He signed it with the date '72'. In 2014 the astronomer Donald Olson used tide tables, weather records and the sun's position to propose about 7:35 a.m. on 13 November 1872, and the Musée Marmottan accepted that date. Earlier scholars who dated the picture to 1873 assumed that Monet was working in Le Havre that spring and that the '72' was mistaken.
entries.source_note: Texas State University press release, 2 Sept 2014, summarising Olson's essay in the Marmottan catalogue Impression, soleil levant: l'histoire vraie du chef-d'œuvre (2014); Marmottan notice 4014.

entries.headline: Monet answers a call for an artists' co-operative
entries.digest: The young critic Paul Alexis wrote in L'Avenir national that artists should organise themselves into a corporation, as workers did. Monet wrote to him that a group of painters gathered at his house had already been discussing such a society. The paper printed his letter. Seven months later the idea became the Société's charter.
entries.source_note: Alexis, L'Avenir national, 5 May 1873, and Monet's reply published there on 12 May 1873, as reproduced in Moffett, The New Painting (1986). Dates from secondary literature; not checked against the newspaper.

entries.headline: The painters sign a company charter
entries.digest: Monet, Renoir, Sisley, Degas, Morisot, Pissarro, Béliard, Guillaumin, Lepic, Levert and Rouart signed the statutes of a co-operative joint-stock company. Members paid an annual share, the society kept a commission on sales, and works were to be hung by size and by lot. The charter set up no jury and no medals. Pissarro had drafted parts of it from the rules of a bakers' co-operative at Pontoise.
entries.source_note: Charter of 27 Dec 1873 as summarised on the Wikiwand/Wikipedia article 'First Impressionist Exhibition' and in Moffett 1986; signer list from the same.

entries.headline: A father's death in the winter of the charter
entries.digest: Morisot's father, Edme-Tiburce Morisot, a senior civil servant, died that January after a long illness. The family letters from the following weeks are about mourning and money. They are also about a widowed mother anxious over her unmarried 33-year-old daughter, who was preparing to send her pictures to an unjuried show of uncertain reputation.
entries.source_note: Rouart (ed.), Correspondance de Berthe Morisot (1950), letters of early 1874; death date from standard biographies, not checked against the civil register.

entries.headline: The society announces an open show
entries.digest: The founding of the society was announced in the arts press, notably La Chronique des arts et de la curiosité. It promised an exhibition with no jury and no prizes. The announcement started a winter of recruiting, with members writing to friends to bring in more exhibitors and more subscriptions.
entries.source_note: NGA, '1874: the birth of Impressionism' (gives 17 January 1874 for the announcement).

entries.headline: News of his father's death in Naples
entries.digest: Auguste De Gas, the banker father who had backed his son's career, died in Naples in February. The family bank turned out to be badly indebted. Within two years Degas was selling pictures and his own collection to cover his brother René's debts. That pressure helps explain why a painter of independent means was suddenly serious about selling.
entries.source_note: Impressionists Gallery Degas chronology ('February 1874, Naples'); family debt crisis in standard biographies (e.g. Loyrette, Degas, 1991).

entries.headline: Duret advises the Salon; Pissarro chooses the company
entries.digest: Pissarro's friend and collector Théodore Duret wrote to him that his next step must be to become known to the public, and that the Salon, with its huge crowds, was the place to do it. He urged him not to bury himself in a small group show. Pissarro, a founder of the society, went ahead with the group regardless.
entries.source_note: Duret to Pissarro, February 1874 (often dated 15 Feb), quoted in Rewald, History of Impressionism; Bailly-Herzberg, Correspondance de Pissarro vol. 1 notes. Day not verified.

entries.headline: Goncourt finds the painter of modern life
entries.digest: Goncourt spent an afternoon in Degas's studio. Degas showed him laundresses at their irons and ballet girls at rehearsal, and he acted out their poses and talked the trade language of the dance and the laundry. Goncourt judged him the artist who had best caught the spirit of modern life of anyone he had yet met. He also noted that Degas seemed nervous, restless and worried about his eyes. He made no mention of the planned exhibition.
entries.source_note: Journal des Goncourt, 2e série vol. 2 (1872–77), entry for 13 février 1874 (Project Gutenberg #17420). Paraphrased; the published text is Edmond's revised version.

entries.headline: Degas presses Tissot to join the realists' show
entries.digest: Degas wrote to James Tissot in London urging him to send work to the boulevard des Capucines without hesitation. He argued that the realist movement no longer needed to fight inside others' exhibitions and should appear as a body on its own walls. He also mentioned that Manet was holding back. Tissot did not exhibit.
entries.source_note: Degas to Tissot, undated, placed in early 1874 in Guérin (ed.), Lettres de Degas (1931/1945). Paraphrase only.

entries.headline: Minette dies nine days before the opening
entries.digest: Pissarro's daughter Jeanne-Rachel, called Minette, his favourite child and his most frequent model, died after a long illness at the age of nine. He had drawn and painted her through her decline and made a lithograph of her as she lay dying. The exhibition opened in Paris within days.
entries.source_note: Clark Art Institute, 'Pissarro's People: Minette'; Kunstmuseum Basel Pissarro biography (1874). Exact day (often given as 6 April) not verified in a primary source.

entries.headline: The Salon jury takes one Manet and refuses two
entries.digest: The 1874 jury accepted 'Le Chemin de fer', which shows a young woman with a book and a puppy beside a little girl at the railings above the Saint-Lazare tracks. It rejected 'Bal masqué à l'Opéra' and a smaller picture. Stéphane Mallarmé published an attack on the jury in Manet's defence. Manet still kept to the Salon and lent no work of his own to the independent show.
entries.source_note: NGA wall texts, Paris 1874 (Railway accepted, Salon no. 1260; Masked Ball rejected); Mallarmé, 'Le Jury de peinture pour 1874 et M. Manet', La Renaissance artistique et littéraire, April 1874 (day not verified).

entries.headline: Hanging the rooms and writing the catalogue
entries.digest: Renoir sat on the hanging committee in Nadar's empty rooms, which were spread over two floors and lined with reddish-brown fabric. His brother Edmond, a journalist, edited the catalogue. Edmond later complained that Monet's titles were all alike, entrances to villages and mornings over towns. By Monet's own account of 1898, Monet told him to put down 'Impression'.
entries.source_note: Upholstery cost and rooms: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page (financial statement; d'Hervilly, Le Rappel, 17 Apr 1874). Title anecdote: Monet's interview with Maurice Guillemot, La Revue illustrée, 15 March 1898 (later recollection).

entries.headline: Doors open: one franc, day and evening
entries.digest: The show opened for a month, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and again from 8 to 10 p.m. under gaslight. Entry cost one franc and the catalogue fifty centimes. It listed 165 numbers by about thirty artists, from Boudin, de Nittis and the etcher Bracquemond to Monet, Degas and Cézanne. Upstairs windows looked straight down onto the crowds of the boulevard.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand 'First Impressionist Exhibition' (hours, prices, catalogue numbering); Ministère de la Culture 1874 page (165 works).

entries.headline: The harbour sunrise hangs as catalogue no. 98
entries.digest: Monet's group included 'Impression, soleil levant', 'Coquelicots' and the big 'Le Déjeuner' of 1868, which the Salon had rejected and which he priced at 5,000 francs, the highest price in the show. He also hung 'Boulevard des Capucines', a view down the very street below, painted from a high window with the crowds as quick dark flecks. Scholars disagree over which of his two versions of it was shown, the one in Kansas City or the one in Moscow.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page (works listed); NGA wall texts (Le Déjeuner, 5,000 francs); Wikiwand on the two Boulevard versions.

entries.headline: 'Le Berceau' on the wall near a modern Olympia
entries.digest: Morisot showed paintings, pastels and watercolours. Among them was 'Le Berceau', in which her sister Edma, in dark clothes, watches her sleeping baby through the white gauze of a cradle curtain. She also showed 'Cache-cache' and views of the coast. Accounts of the hanging put her painting not far from Cézanne's 'Une moderne Olympia', the show's loudest picture.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page; NGA wall texts (The Cradle and Hide-and-Seek shown); Hérodote (Berceau near Olympia).

entries.headline: A hanged man's house and a new Olympia
entries.digest: Cézanne showed three pictures. 'La Maison du pendu' is a thickly worked Auvers lane, with roofs and walls stacked against each other in crusty paint. 'Une moderne Olympia' is a small, feverish sketch: a black servant whips a white sheet off a crouching nude, while a top-hatted man, often read as the painter himself, looks on. The third was a landscape study of Auvers.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page; NGA wall texts (Hanged Man's House probably no. 44); Musée d'Orsay collection records 1476 and 1478.

entries.headline: Dancers, racecourses and a laundress
entries.digest: Degas sent ten works, including 'Classe de danse', 'Répétition de ballet' and 'Aux courses en province', where a family in a carriage drives past a country racecourse. Several were the subjects Goncourt had admired in the studio two months before. Critics who disliked Monet's sketchiness often made an exception for Degas's drawing.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page (Degas, 10 works; titles); NGA wall texts (dates of the pictures).

entries.headline: 'La Loge': a woman in stripes at the theatre
entries.digest: Renoir's 'La Loge' (catalogue no. 142) shows a woman in a black-and-white striped gown, with a rose at her breast, leaning forward from a theatre box. Behind her a man in evening dress has raised his opera glasses toward the other boxes rather than the stage. The models were the model Nini Lopez and Renoir's brother Edmond. He also showed a dancer and a Parisienne.
entries.source_note: Courtauld Gallery record P.1948.SC.338; NGA wall texts (no. 142).

entries.headline: Hoar-frost and orchards from Pontoise
entries.digest: Pissarro showed five landscapes, among them 'Gelée blanche', a ploughed hillside furred with frost under a low winter sun, along with an orchard and a June morning. Leroy's satirical painter would later look at the frost picture and see only scrapings of palette on a dirty canvas.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page (titles); Leroy, Le Charivari, 25 Apr 1874 (the frost joke).

entries.headline: A republican critic praises the independent show
entries.digest: Burty reviewed the show in Gambetta's paper as a serious, self-financed venture by working artists. He described the sight of pictures hung where the life of the boulevard could be seen from the windows, and he praised the painters' fresh light. He also took the printmakers seriously, as few other critics did.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page cites Burty, La République française, 24 April 1874; other studies give 16 or 25 April. Content summarised from secondary accounts.

entries.headline: 'L'Exposition des impressionnistes': a satire coins a name
entries.digest: Leroy described a visit to the rooms with an imaginary old landscape painter, Joseph Vincent, a pupil of Bertin decorated by several governments. The old man's mind gives way room by room. He finds Pissarro's frost to be palette scrapings and Monet's boulevard crowds to be black dribbles. At the harbour picture he cries that wallpaper in its first state is more finished than this 'impression'. At the end he dances in front of a guard, taking him for a portrait. From the title on, Leroy called the whole group 'impressionists'.
entries.source_note: Le Charivari, 25 April 1874 (Gallica); summarised on Wikiwand and the Ministère de la Culture 1874 page. Paraphrased; no translation quoted.

entries.headline: Castagnary takes the joke word and defines it
entries.digest: Writing four days after Leroy, Castagnary called the exhibitors impressionists in the sense that they painted the sensation a landscape produces, not the landscape itself. He praised their wit and lightness of touch. He also warned that this was a narrow principle. Within a few years, he predicted, the stronger talents would move on and the group would break up, some of them heading back to the Salon.
entries.source_note: Le Siècle, 29 April 1874; core sentence cited in French on Hérodote; date confirmed in NGA wall texts. Paraphrased.

entries.headline: Her old teacher's alarm reaches her mother
entries.digest: Joseph Guichard had taught Berthe and Edma drawing as girls. He visited the rooms and wrote at once to Madame Morisot that his heart sank to see her daughter's work in such harmful company. He urged that Berthe break with these people before her reputation suffered, and he said that a Salon showing would repair matters. Madame Morisot passed on the warning. Berthe went on exhibiting with the group for most of the rest of her life.
entries.source_note: Guichard to Mme Morisot, undated (April 1874), in Rouart (ed.), Correspondance de Berthe Morisot; key phrase cited on Hérodote. Paraphrased.

entries.headline: A count buys 'La Maison du pendu'
entries.digest: The collector Count Armand Doria bought 'La Maison du pendu' from the show, one of only a handful of sales. Most reviewers had made Cézanne the butt of their jokes, and Leroy's mad old painter treated 'Une moderne Olympia' as the final outrage. The sale was the first real sign that his difficult surfaces could find a buyer.
entries.source_note: Provenance in the Musée d'Orsay record 1476 (Doria; price commonly given as 300 francs, not verified here); Hérodote (only four works sold).

entries.headline: The Salon opens with 'Le Chemin de fer'
entries.digest: The official Salon opened with more than 3,600 works, and over the next two months its catalogue sold nearly 49,000 copies. Manet's single accepted picture drew caricatures and jokes. The medal of honour went to Gérôme, and much of the attention went to Mercié's 'Gloria Victis'. Manet had preferred to be laughed at here rather than at the boulevard des Capucines.
entries.source_note: Hérodote (opening 1 May, 3,657 works, Gérôme); NGA wall texts (48,766 catalogues; Railway no. 1260).

entries.headline: To Duret: the show is a success
entries.digest: Pissarro wrote to Duret, the friend who had told him to stick to the Salon, that the exhibition was going well and was a success. He admitted that the critics were tearing them to pieces and accusing them of not studying. He said he was going back to work regardless.
entries.source_note: Pissarro to Duret, 5 May 1874, Bailly-Herzberg, Correspondance vol. 1; cited on the Ministère de la Culture 1874 page.

entries.headline: The doors close after a month
entries.digest: The exhibition closed after about 3,500 paid visits, a tiny number beside the Salon's crowds across the city. Only four works are recorded as sold. Some sixty notices had appeared in the press, mostly in republican and left-leaning papers. Ernest Chesneau had predicted an autumn show, but none followed.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page (closing date; Chesneau, Paris-Journal 7 May); Hérodote (3,500 visitors, four sales, about sixty articles); NGA.

entries.headline: The accounts: rent, upholstery, police, catalogues
entries.digest: The society's financial statement listed 2,020 francs in rent for Nadar's rooms, about 3,340 francs for upholstery and hangings, and nearly 1,000 for lighting. It recorded 141 francs paid to the sergents de ville who kept order, and 742 francs to print a catalogue that sold only about 320 copies. Receipts from tickets, catalogues and commissions came to just over 10,000 francs, and expenses just over 9,000. Members' unpaid shares hung over everything.
entries.source_note: Financial statement of 27 May 1874, figures as given on the Ministère de la Culture 1874 page; totals (10,221.50 and 9,272.20 francs) as on Wikiwand.

entries.headline: Painting outdoors beside Monet and Renoir
entries.digest: Staying with his family at Gennevilliers across the Seine, Manet spent the summer painting beside Monet at Argenteuil, and Renoir joined them. One afternoon Manet painted Monet's wife Camille and their son in the garden, and Renoir set up beside him and painted the same group. Manet had kept out of their exhibition, but that summer his own palette lightened toward theirs.
entries.source_note: Standard Manet chronologies (Cachin et al., Manet 1832–1883, 1983); Manet's 'The Monet Family in Their Garden' (Met) and Renoir's companion picture (NGA). Exact days unknown.

entries.headline: A son born as the money runs out
entries.digest: Julie Vellay gave birth to their son Félix that summer, three months after Minette's death. The exhibition had brought in almost nothing. By autumn the family went to stay with Pissarro's friend Ludovic Piette at Montfoucault in the Mayenne, where living cost less, and Pissarro painted farmyards and peasants there through the winter.
entries.source_note: Kunstmuseum Basel Pissarro biography (financial strain, Montfoucault 1874); Félix's birth date (24 July 1874) from standard chronologies, not verified here.

entries.headline: A summer by the sea and a proposal
entries.digest: Morisot spent the summer on the Normandy coast near the Manet family. Eugène Manet, Édouard's quieter younger brother and himself a painter, courted her there. Her letters to her sister from these weeks describe the boredom and freedom of the shore, beach pictures begun and abandoned, and her doubts about marriage.
entries.source_note: Rouart (ed.), Correspondance de Berthe Morisot, summer 1874 letters (undated or partially dated).

entries.headline: To his mother: Pissarro thinks well of me
entries.digest: Cézanne wrote to his mother in Aix that Pissarro had a good opinion of him, and that he had a very good one of himself. He said he was beginning to find himself stronger than those around him. He added that he must keep working, not to reach the polished finish that fools admire, but to finish things as truth demanded. It was his answer, five months on, to the laughter at the boulevard des Capucines.
entries.source_note: Cézanne to his mother, 26 September 1874, in Rewald (ed.), Correspondance. Paraphrased from the French.

entries.headline: The members vote to dissolve the company
entries.digest: Renoir called the shareholders to a general meeting in his studio and chaired it. The accounts showed that once debts were paid only about 278 francs remained, against more than 3,700 francs of liabilities. Each member would owe about 185 francs. The meeting voted unanimously to liquidate, and members who had already paid the next year's share were refunded.
entries.source_note: Minutes of the general meeting, 17 December 1874, as summarised on the Ministère de la Culture 1874 page (unanimous liquidation) and Wikiwand (Renoir convened; figures).

entries.headline: Berthe Morisot marries Eugène Manet
entries.digest: Five days after the society was dissolved, Morisot married Eugène Manet in a quiet ceremony while the family was still in mourning. The marriage settled the question her mother had worried over all year. It also gave her a husband who backed her work and her place among the independents, and she kept signing her pictures 'Berthe Morisot'.
entries.source_note: Standard Morisot chronologies (e.g. Musée d'Orsay/Barnes 2018–19 catalogue); Rouart (ed.), Correspondance.

entries.headline: A preface for a desperate auction
entries.digest: With the society wound up and money short, Monet, Renoir, Sisley and Morisot put 73 works up for auction at the Hôtel Drouot. Burty wrote the catalogue preface. He presented the pictures as small mirrors of the open air and of modern pleasures, and he asked buyers to judge them for themselves.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1876 page (24 March 1875, 73 works, Burty preface); content of the preface summarised from secondary accounts.

entries.headline: Jeers in the saleroom and the police called
entries.digest: Durand-Ruel acted as expert for the sale with the auctioneer Charles Pillet. In his memoirs, written decades later, he recalled jeering at every bid, and quarrels so heated that Pillet had to send for the police to keep them from turning into fights. Théodore Duret later put the total raised at no more than about 10,350 francs.
entries.source_note: Durand-Ruel, memoirs (in Venturi, Les Archives de l'impressionnisme, 1939), as cited on the Ministère de la Culture 1876 page; Duret's total from the same page. Memoir written later.

entries.headline: Her 'Intérieur' fetches the top price
entries.digest: Amid the jeering, Morisot's 'Intérieur' of 1872 sold for 480 francs, the highest price of the day. Many canvases by her male colleagues went for around a hundred francs or were bought in. She had stood at the centre of the scandal of 1874, and the market was kinder to her than to the others.
entries.source_note: ArtExplora Academy, 'The Art Market' (Interior, 480 francs, top price; canvases about 100 francs).

entries.headline: Renoir's auction and a new collector
entries.digest: The sale had been Renoir's idea, and his canvases fetched some of the lowest prices, several barely covering their frames. In the room or soon after, the customs official Victor Chocquet saw his work. Chocquet wrote to ask Renoir to paint his wife, and he became one of the group's most loyal collectors and later bought Cézanne.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1876 page (Renoir instigated the sale); Chocquet episode from Vollard and Rewald (later accounts).

entries.headline: Twenty canvases sold for almost nothing
entries.digest: Monet's landscapes went for prices that hardly paid for his paint. The year before, Ernest Hoschedé, a department-store owner and collector, had bought 'Impression, soleil levant' itself. In the summer after the sale Monet was writing to friends, including Manet, for loans of a few francs to keep the household going at Argenteuil.
entries.source_note: ArtExplora Academy (Hoschedé bought Impression in 1874; low prices); Monet's begging letters of 1875 in Wildenstein's catalogue raisonné (summary).

entries.place: Paris, for Le Sémaphore de Marseille
entries.headline: Zola tells Marseille about the brawl at Drouot
entries.digest: In his Paris letter for a Marseille paper, Zola described the auction as stormy. He thought the bidders and scoffers had even come to blows. He treated the uproar as further proof of how hard it was for these painters to get a hearing. He did not sign the column, as was usual for this work.
entries.source_note: Le Sémaphore de Marseille, 27 March 1875, cited (with a short French phrase) on the Ministère de la Culture 1876 page.

entries.place: Cowes and Ryde, Isle of Wight
entries.headline: Honeymoon summer, painting yachts at Cowes
entries.digest: With Eugène, Morisot spent part of the summer on the Isle of Wight. She tried to paint harbour scenes and people on the shore, and complained in her letters home that her models would not stay still and that the English stared. She sent home sketches and impressions of English manners. The resulting pictures went into the second group show.
entries.source_note: Rouart (ed.), Correspondance de Berthe Morisot, letters from Cowes and Ryde, 1875; 'Isle of Wight' pictures shown 1876.

entries.headline: With Rouart, inviting Caillebotte to the second show
entries.digest: Renoir and Henri Rouart wrote to the young painter Gustave Caillebotte with the plan for a new exhibition. Durand-Ruel had rented them two rooms, including the large one. The show would open on 20 March and run a month, each exhibitor would pay 120 francs, and no one could hang more than five works. In the event both the date and the limit slipped.
entries.source_note: Renoir and Rouart to Caillebotte, 5 February 1876, cited on the Ministère de la Culture 1876 page.

entries.headline: Twelve landscapes in the last room
entries.digest: Pissarro showed twelve pictures, hung together in the last of the three rooms. They included the Montfoucault farm scenes painted in the hard winter after the first show. The company he had designed was gone, but the group exhibition went on, and he would be the only painter to show at all eight.
entries.source_note: Kunstmuseum Basel Pissarro biography (1876: twelve pictures, last of three galleries); Ministère de la Culture 1876 page.

entries.date_display: Early April 1876 (opening given as 30 March or 1 April)
entries.headline: Degas hangs the New Orleans cotton office
entries.digest: At the second exhibition, held in three rooms of Durand-Ruel's gallery, Degas showed more than twenty works. Among them was the portrait group of his uncle's cotton office in New Orleans: men in black reading newspapers, testing samples of white cotton and leaning on the counters. Nineteen artists took part, and Caillebotte now joined them. Cézanne stayed away.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1876 page (venue, 19 participants, Degas 24 works); Impressionists Gallery chronology (opening 30 March, 22 works); Cotton Office shown 1876 per standard Degas literature.

entries.headline: Camille in a Japanese robe
entries.digest: Among Monet's eighteen or nineteen works at the second show was the life-size 'La Japonaise'. In it Camille, in a blonde wig, turns in a scarlet kimono embroidered with a samurai, against a wall scattered with Japanese paper fans. The picture traded on the fashion for Japanese goods that had flooded Paris since Japan opened its ports. Critics found it a showpiece rather than a sincere work.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1876 page (Monet 19 works); La Japonaise (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston) exhibited 1876 per MFA records and standard literature.

entries.headline: Le Figaro's Wolff: lunatics, one of them a woman
entries.digest: Albert Wolff's notice in Le Figaro, the most hostile of the season, called the exhibitors a handful of madmen led by ambition, one of whom was a woman. Everyone knew he meant Morisot. She had seventeen works on the walls. Family tradition has it that Eugène Manet was so angry that he had to be talked out of challenging Wolff.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1876 page (Wolff, Le Figaro, 3 April 1876; Morisot 17 works); Eugène Manet's reaction is family tradition reported in Morisot biographies, not a dated document.

entries.headline: Explaining the 'Intransigeants' to English readers
entries.digest: Burty sent a report on the second show to the London weekly The Academy under the title 'The Exhibition of the Intransigeants'. He took the French press's insult for the group and tried to explain to a British audience what these painters were after, with particular attention to Degas.
entries.source_note: Degas catalogue raisonné (Schulman), bibliography no. 136: Burty, 'The Exhibition of the Intransigeants', London, 15 April 1876. Content summarised; text not consulted.

entries.headline: Manet's own show of his rejected pictures
entries.digest: The Salon jury had rejected both of Manet's 1876 entries, 'Le Linge' and a portrait of the engraver Desboutin. Rather than join his friends at Durand-Ruel's, he opened his own studio to the public from 15 April to 1 May. Cards invited visitors to judge for themselves, and crowds came. Even now his independent stand was a one-man affair.
entries.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1876 page (Manet rejected; studio show 15 April–1 May 1876).

entries.headline: Zola explains the 'impressionists' to Russian readers
entries.digest: In his monthly letter on 'two art exhibitions in May' for the St Petersburg review, Zola set the group's show at Durand-Ruel's against the Salon. He named Monet as the most distinctive talent and described the painters as the true naturalists of the open air. He called them a group of revolutionaries and accepted Leroy's joke as their name.
entries.source_note: Zola, 'Deux expositions d'art au mois de mai', Le Messager de l'Europe (Vestnik Evropy), June 1876, in Zola, Écrits sur l'art. Summary from secondary literature.

claims.claim: Paints the Le Havre harbour sunrise later titled 'Impression, soleil levant'; date contested (signed '72'; Olson/Marmottan 2014 propose 13 Nov 1872; earlier catalogues 1873)
claims.evidence: Signature and date on canvas; Olson in Marmottan catalogue 2014; TXST press release

convergences.label: The charter is signed
convergences.note: Six of the chapter's painters put their names to one legal document. Pissarro saw it as a workers' co-operative, Degas as a showcase for realism with respectable allies, and Monet as a way to sell. Morisot signed as a woman of good family in a venture her family and teacher distrusted.

convergences.label: A winter of mourning and recruiting
convergences.note: Morisot and Degas both lost their fathers in the weeks before the show, and Degas's loss came with family debts. Goncourt, in the studio, saw only an inspired painter of laundresses. Duret was advising Pissarro to stay with the Salon.

convergences.label: Opening day at 35 boulevard des Capucines
convergences.note: The same rooms held Morisot's quiet cradle, Cézanne's raucous Olympia, Degas's dancers, Renoir's theatre box and Monet's misty harbour. The rules hung them by size and by lot, so the pictures sat side by side whatever their makers thought of one another.

convergences.label: The week of the reviews (24–30 April)
convergences.note: Within six days a friendly republican critic praised the show and a satirist mocked it under a nickname. A second republican critic then turned the nickname into a definition, while Morisot's old teacher wrote privately to her mother in alarm. One word changed meaning in four days.

convergences.label: The Salon opens across town
convergences.note: Manet's railway picture drew Salon crowds of a size the cooperative never saw. Four days later Pissarro wrote that their own little show was a success, and the society's accounts tell a third version of how it went.

convergences.label: Dissolution and a wedding (17–22 December)
convergences.note: In one week the company was voted out of existence in Renoir's studio and Morisot married Manet's brother. The two families of 1874, the exhibitors and the Manets, became bound together just as the formal society ended.

convergences.label: The auction at the Hôtel Drouot
convergences.note: Burty's preface asked for fair judgement. Durand-Ruel remembered the police being called, and Zola wrote for Marseille that blows were struck. Morisot's picture made the best price of the day while Renoir's and Monet's went for next to nothing.

convergences.label: The second exhibition and its critics (April 1876)
convergences.note: Degas brought his New Orleans cotton office and Monet his Japonaise to rue Le Peletier. Wolff mocked Morisot as the woman among madmen, and Burty explained the group to London. Manet opened his own studio to show his Salon rejects, and Zola reported to St Petersburg.

ties.note: Manet's friend and model since 1868, Morisot became his sister-in-law on 22 December 1874. She exhibited with the group that he refused to join.
Old friends and rivals from the Café Guerbois. Degas tried and failed to recruit Manet for 1874.
Cézanne painted beside Pissarro at Pontoise and Auvers in 1872–74. Pissarro insisted on his inclusion, and Cézanne cited Pissarro's good opinion to his mother.
Close friends who painted the same motifs side by side. In summer 1874 they worked together at Argenteuil, with Manet beside them.
Manet painted Monet's family at Argenteuil in 1874 and lent him money in the hard year after the Drouot sale.
Leroy's satire took Monet's catalogue title as the name for the whole group.
Four days apart, the two critics used the same word for opposite purposes, one as mockery and one as definition.
Goncourt visited Degas's studio on 13 February 1874 and recorded his laundresses and dancers in the Journal.
Fellow collectors of Japanese prints and regulars in each other's circles. Burty appears often in the Goncourt Journal.
Boyhood friends from the college at Aix. Zola wrote about the group for distant readers while Cézanne was its most derided member.
Zola had defended Manet in print since 1866, and Manet painted his portrait in 1868.
Dealer and painter since they met in London in 1871. Durand-Ruel's 1873 slump in purchases pushed Monet toward the co-operative.
The society's last general meeting was held in Renoir's studio, 35 rue Saint-Georges, and Renoir chaired it.

threads_out.note: After Perry's ships forced Japan's ports open in 1853–54, prints, fans and kimonos poured into Paris. Burty, who is usually credited with coining 'japonisme' in 1872, and Goncourt collected them. Monet hung 'La Japonaise' in the 1876 show, and his Le Havre harbour picture is often compared with the flattened views of Japanese prints.

The Vienna Secession's sixteenth exhibition (1903) was a survey of the development of Impressionism. It brought Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro and Morisot to the city where Klimt's circle was breaking with its own academy, much as the Société anonyme had broken with the Salon.

Monet, the painter of the 1874 'Impression', spent the war years at Giverny painting the great Water Lilies decorations. He offered them to the French state as a monument to peace the day after the Armistice of 11 November 1918.

images.title: Impression, soleil levant
images.caption: Monet's view of Le Havre harbour at sunrise: blue-grey cranes and masts, a dark rowing boat, an orange sun and its broken reflection. Shown as no. 98 in 1874 and the source of Leroy's joke name. The date of painting is debated (signed '72').
images.credit: Claude Monet; Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris

images.title: Le Berceau
images.caption: Morisot's sister Edma watching her sleeping baby through a gauze cradle curtain. It hung in the 1874 show, the year her teacher wrote that she was in harmful company.

images.title: La Maison du pendu, Auvers-sur-Oise
images.caption: Cézanne's thickly built-up lane at Auvers, painted while he worked beside Pissarro. One of the few works sold from the 1874 exhibition.

images.title: Une moderne Olympia
images.caption: Cézanne's small, feverish reworking of Manet's Olympia, with a top-hatted spectator. The picture the 1874 critics mocked most.

images.title: La Loge
images.caption: Renoir's woman in a striped gown in a theatre box, her companion's opera glasses turned to the audience. Modelled by Nini Lopez and Edmond Renoir, shown in 1874 as no. 142.

images.title: Boulevard des Capucines
images.caption: Monet's view down the boulevard from a high window near Nadar's studio, with crowds as quick dark strokes. One of two versions, and it is debated whether this or the Moscow canvas hung in 1874.
images.credit: Claude Monet; Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City
